# Affordability Gaps {#sec-gaps}

<!-- Purpose: affordability by income band, tenure, and geography — what each AMI band can
     afford, who is cost-burdened, and how the supply of affordable rentals and for-sale
     listings measures against need (PLAN.md §7 Ch 4).
     Narrative: prose migrated from the team's Google Doc draft (Oct 2026); numbers audited against the data. -->

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")

gaps    <- read_rds("data/gaps.rds")
chas    <- read_rds("data/chas.rds")
costs   <- read_rds("data/acs_costs.rds")
hud_ami <- read_rds("data/hud_ami.rds")
mls     <- read_rds("data/mls.rds")

# Palette anchors (match ggtext subtitle spans to fill/line colors)
blue   <- hda_pal[1]
green  <- hda_pal[2]
yellow <- hda_pal[3]
coral  <- hda_pal[4]

geo_label <- function(code, geo_type = NA) case_when(
  code == fauquier   ~ "Fauquier County",
  code == "5183136"  ~ "Warrenton",
  code == "5105336"  ~ "Bealeton",
  code == virginia   ~ "Virginia",
  TRUE               ~ NA_character_
)

# AMI income-band factor (short ordered labels; CHAS T7/T8 already use these strings)
band_lvls <- c("≤30% AMI", "30-50% AMI", "50-80% AMI", "80-100% AMI", ">100% AMI")
# Display-only en dashes (band values stay hyphenated: scope_ladder() matches on them)
band_en <- \(x) str_replace(x, "(\\d)-(\\d)", "\\1–\\2")

# --- Inline scalars for bullet text ----------------------------------------

# HUD AMI (4-person reference column)
mfi <- hud_ami$mfi
ami4 <- hud_ami$ami |> filter(hh_size == "4-person")
ami80_4  <- ami4$income[ami4$level == "ami80"]
ami100_4 <- ami4$income[ami4$level == "ami100"]

# What a 50% AMI household can afford (gaps$afford_by_band, precomputed — no recompute)
ab <- gaps$afford_by_band
afford50_rent  <- ab$max_rent[ab$band == "ami50"]
afford50_price <- ab$max_price[ab$band == "ami50"]
# Rent anchor = ACS median gross rent (DATA-AUDIT.md C1, Jonathan-approved 2026-07-28):
# full rental universe, highest reliability. CoStar/MLS are supplemental context, not this figure.
med_price   <- gaps$income_needed$med_price     # 650,000
med_rent    <- gaps$income_needed$med_rent      # 1,613 (ACS B25064)
costar_rent <- gaps$income_needed$costar_rent   # latest CoStar quarter, market-rate apartments, nominal
mls_rent    <- gaps$income_needed$mls_rent      # MLS broker-side closed-lease median (2025)

# ACS burden (multi-year trend frame; county 2024 = 40.2% / 21.5%)
bt <- costs$burden_trend
bt_c <- bt |> filter(GEOID == fauquier)
acs_rent_24  <- bt_c$share[bt_c$tenure == "Renter" & bt_c$year == 2024]   # 0.402
acs_rent_13  <- bt_c$share[bt_c$tenure == "Renter" & bt_c$year == 2013]   # 0.440
acs_own_24   <- bt_c$share[bt_c$tenure == "Owner"  & bt_c$year == 2024]   # 0.215
acs_own_13   <- bt_c$share[bt_c$tenure == "Owner"  & bt_c$year == 2013]   # 0.287

# CHAS T8 burden (county) — burdened = cost-burdened + severely; drop "No or negative income"
t8_burden <- chas$t8 |>
  filter(cost_burden != "No or negative income") |>
  summarize(
    share = sum(estimate[cost_burden != "Not cost-burdened"]) / sum(estimate),
    .by = c(geo_code, tenure)
  )
chas_rent <- t8_burden$share[t8_burden$geo_code == fauquier & t8_burden$tenure == "Renter"]  # .329
chas_own  <- t8_burden$share[t8_burden$geo_code == fauquier & t8_burden$tenure == "Homeowner"] # .201

# Rental gap (gaps$rental_gap — precomputed; 4 bands)
rg <- gaps$rental_gap
rg_deficit_30  <- rg$surplus_deficit[rg$band == "≤30% AMI"]   # -625
rg_deficit_tot <- sum(rg$surplus_deficit)

# Ownership gap (gaps$ownership_gap — precomputed by r/gaps.R from mls$active; 5 bands, listings
# incremental → sum = number of active for-sale listings in the snapshot)
og <- gaps$ownership_gap
og_total_listings <- sum(og$listings_affordable)
og_below_100 <- sum(og$listings_affordable[og$band %in% c("ami30","ami50","ami80","ami100")])
og_top_band  <- og$listings_affordable[og$band == "ami120"]
og_lower_txt <- paste(og$listings_affordable[og$band %in% c("ami30","ami50","ami80","ami100")], collapse = ", ")  # e.g. "0, 1, 3, 7"
og_asof      <- format(max(mls$active$snapshot_date), "%B %Y")

# Market check on the CHAS rental gap: share of MLS closed leases at or below the 50% AMI rent
# (same lease-price screen as r/gaps.R)
lease_50 <- mls$rentals |>
  filter(between(lease_price, 200, 15000)) |>
  summarize(share = mean(lease_price <= afford50_rent), .by = year) |>
  arrange(year)
l50 <- \(y) lease_50$share[lease_50$year == y]

# Wages vs costs (gaps$wages_costs — precomputed)
wc <- gaps$wages_costs
wage_all    <- wc$avg_wage[wc$category == "All Jobs"]
wage_retail <- wc$avg_wage[wc$category == "Retail Trade"]
wage_health <- wc$avg_wage[wc$category == "Health Care"]
wage_gov    <- wc$avg_wage[wc$category == "Local Government"]
inc_rent <- gaps$income_needed$renter_income   # 64,520 (ACS-anchored)
inc_buy  <- gaps$income_needed$buyer_income    # 204,891

# T7 total occupied households (detail-sum benchmark ≈ 25,944)
t7_total_hh <- chas$t7 |> filter(geo_code == fauquier) |> pull(estimate) |> sum()
```

## What sets the standard: Area Median Income

For affordability, it is typical to use the "Area Median Income" (AMI) benchmark. Fauquier is part of the Washington, D.C. metro income-limit area, whose published median family income is `r label_dollar()(mfi)` annually. This metric is far above what local wages (@fig-wages-costs) would suggest.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ami
#| tbl-cap: "Fauquier's income limits are set by the high-cost D.C. metro area"
#| tbl-alt: "Table of HUD income limits for Fauquier County by AMI level (30%, 50%, 80%, 100%, 120%) and household size from 1 to 8 persons. Dollar limits rise with household size and with AMI level. The 80% limit is capped to the national median, so the step from 80% to 100% AMI is far larger than the steps before it."

ami_wide <- hud_ami$ami |>
  mutate(
    level = factor(level, levels = c("ami30","ami50","ami80","ami100","ami120"),
                   labels = c("30% AMI","50% AMI","80% AMI","100% AMI","120% AMI")),
    hh = str_remove(hh_size, "-person")
  ) |>
  transmute(level, hh, income = label_dollar()(income)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = hh, values_from = income) |>
  arrange(level)

ami_wide |>
  kbl(align = "lrrrrrrrr",
      col.names = c("Income limit", paste0(1:8, "-person"))) |>
  kable_styling(c("condensed", "striped"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Household size" = 8)) |>
  footnote(
    general = tbl_note(paste0(
      ami_cap(),
      "<br>**Notes:** Limits for the ", hud_ami$area_name,
      " (published median family income ", label_dollar()(mfi), "). ",
      hud_ami$cap_note, "."
    )),
    general_title = "", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE, escape = FALSE
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## HUD's 80% income cap
HUD caps the 80% income limit at the national median, so in the D.C. metro the 80% limit sits lower than its usual spacing from the 50% limit would suggest. The large jump from 80% to 100% AMI is an artifact of that cap, not a data error.
:::

In other words, for a 4-person household, 80% AMI is `r label_dollar()(ami80_4)` and 100% AMI is `r label_dollar()(ami100_4)`. These are the reference points behind the affordability thresholds used throughout this chapter. Additionally, these are the income benchmarks that housing programs throughout Fauquier must use.

## What each income band can afford

```{r}
#| label: tbl-afford-band
#| tbl-cap: "Even a middle-income household is priced well below the county's median home"
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Table showing, for each AMI band from 30% to 120%, the household income, the maximum affordable monthly rent, and the maximum affordable home purchase price. A 50% AMI household can afford about ", label_dollar()(afford50_rent), " in rent and a ", label_dollar(accuracy = 1000)(afford50_price), " home; only the 120% AMI band approaches the county''s median sale price.")'

ab_tbl <- gaps$afford_by_band |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, levels = c("ami30","ami50","ami80","ami100","ami120"),
                        labels = c("30% AMI","50% AMI","80% AMI","100% AMI","120% AMI"))) |>
  transmute(
    Band = band,
    `Household income` = label_dollar()(income),
    `Max affordable rent` = label_dollar()(round(max_rent, -1)),
    `Max affordable purchase price` = label_dollar()(round(max_price, -3))
  )

asm <- gaps$assumptions
ab_tbl |>
  kbl(align = "lrrr") |>
  kable_styling(c("condensed", "striped"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  footnote(
    general = tbl_note(paste0(
      "**Sources:** HUD Section 8 Income Limits, FY2026. Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, ",
      format(asm$rate_pull_date, "%B %Y"), ". HDAdvisors affordability calculation.",
      "<br>**Notes:** Rent is affordable at 30% of gross income. Rents are rounded to $10 and purchase prices to $1,000. Purchase price assumes a ",
      label_percent(accuracy = 0.01)(asm$mortgage_rate), " 30-year fixed rate, ",
      label_percent(accuracy = 1)(asm$down_payment), " down, a ",
      label_percent(accuracy = 1)(asm$front_end_ratio), " front-end ratio, and ",
      label_dollar()(asm$tax_ins_monthly), "/month taxes and insurance, for a ",
      asm$representative_hh_size, " household."
    )),
    general_title = "", footnote_as_chunk = TRUE, escape = FALSE
  )
```

For context, a 50% AMI household can only afford about `r label_dollar()(afford50_rent)` in housing costs, which falls within the modal rent band between $1,500 and $1,999 and is slightly above the ACS median gross rent of `r label_dollar()(med_rent)`. It is below the `r label_dollar()(mls_rent)` median MLS closed lease, which skews toward larger broker-listed homes. This household could buy a home of roughly `r label_dollar()(afford50_price)`, a fraction of the `r label_dollar()(med_price)` median sale price, and widely unavailable throughout the county.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees raised questions about the quality of aging apartments across the county, along with limited availability. Finding a family-sized rental that does not exceed `r label_dollar()(afford50_rent)` would be a challenge, and pairing quality with affordability was described as "winning the lottery."
:::

Greater affordability rises steeply with increased household income: only at 100–120% AMI does the affordable purchase price clear a quarter-million dollars. Even an affordable purchase price for a household at 120% AMI is `r label_dollar()(ab$max_price[ab$band=="ami120"])`, short of the county median sales price at `r label_dollar()(med_price)`.

These thresholds, and not local wages, define who the market can and cannot serve; the gaps that follow measure the distance between them.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## A note on "median rent"

This chapter anchors on the **ACS median gross rent (`r label_dollar()(med_rent)`)** — it covers the full universe of occupied rentals and carries the highest reliability of any rent figure in this study (@sec-market-rental). Two other figures appear elsewhere and mean something different: **CoStar's asking rent at market-rate apartment communities (`r label_dollar()(round(costar_rent))`)** tracks only professionally managed market-rate properties, and the **MLS closed-lease median (`r label_dollar()(mls_rent)`)** reflects broker-side leases, which skew toward larger single-family homes and townhouses rather than the smaller units that make up most of the rental stock — not a market-wide asking rent.
:::

## Who bears the cost: households by income and tenure

The divide of housing tenure, renting vs. owning, is ultimately a division of income. Low-income households skew heavily toward renting. Renters are a large share of all households in both the county's 30% and below and 30-50% AMI bands. Owners dominate in the above 80% AMI bands across the county, Warrenton, and Bealeton.

Overall, Warrenton carries a higher renter share across every income band, consistent with its role as the county's principal rental submarket. Bealeton's cells are small and are read as counts, not precise rates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hh-band-tenure
#| fig-cap: "Renters cluster at the lowest incomes while owners dominate the top bands"
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart of households by AMI income band and tenure for Fauquier County, Warrenton, and Bealeton. In the county, renters make up a large share of households in the two lowest income bands but a small share above 80% AMI, where owners dominate. Warrenton has a higher renter share across bands. Bealeton's town cells are small and should be read as counts."

hh_bt <- chas$t7 |>
  summarize(estimate = sum(estimate), moe = sqrt(sum(moe^2)),
            .by = c(geo_code, sumlev, household_income, tenure)) |>
  mutate(
    cv = if_else(estimate > 0, (moe / 1.645) / estimate * 100, NA_real_),
    band = factor(household_income, levels = band_lvls),
    tenure = factor(if_else(tenure == "Homeowner", "Owner", "Renter"),
                    levels = c("Renter", "Owner")),
    geo = factor(geo_label(geo_code),
                 levels = c("Fauquier County", "Warrenton", "Bealeton"))
  ) |>
  flag_reliability()

ggplot(hh_bt, aes(band, estimate, fill = tenure)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  facet_wrap(~ geo, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Renter = coral, Owner = blue)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = band_en) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title = "Renters cluster at the lowest incomes while owners dominate the top bands",
    subtitle = "Households by income band: <span style='color:#e76f52'>**renters**</span> vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**owners**</span>",
    caption = paste0(chas_cap("T7"),
                     "<br>**Note:** Town cells reflect small samples. Read them as counts, not precise rates."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.subtitle = element_markdown(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7, angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Data note: CHAS universe
CHAS detail sums to roughly `r format(round(t7_total_hh/100)*100, big.mark = ",")` occupied households county-wide. This is the denominator behind the burden and gap figures that follow.
:::

## Cost burden over time (ACS)

::: {.callout-warning}
## Definition: cost burden
Cost burden is defined as paying more than 30% of household income towards housing costs. This is an important and widely tracked metric, as it can help identify both reasonable payment benchmarks across income bands and help to identify vulnerabilities in the housing market.
:::

Renters in Fauquier are consistently the more cost burdened group: about `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_rent_24)` of renters were cost-burdened in 2024 versus `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_own_24)` of owners. This is a gap of nearly 20 points that has held across the decade.

Luckily, burden has edged down recently, not up. Since 2013 renter cost burden has moved from `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_rent_13)` down to `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_rent_24)`, while owner cost burden has moved from `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_own_13)` to `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_own_24)` over the same time period. This could reflect income growth and refinancing opportunities during the low-rate decade. That said, these burden levels remain high, especially for renters, and the recent rate environment increases for owners (@sec-market-ownership) points in the opposite direction for overall relief.

```{r}
#| label: fig-burden-trend
#| fig-cap: "Cost burden has eased since 2013 but renters remain far more burdened"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the share of cost-burdened households in Fauquier County at four data years (2013, 2017, 2021 and 2024), split by tenure, with 2024 town points. The renter burden line declines gently from about 44% to 40%, staying well above the owner line, which falls from about 29% to 22%. In 2024, Warrenton and Bealeton renter points sit above the county renter line at roughly 55% and 59%, while the two towns' owner points sit near the county owner line at about 19% and 27%."

trend_c <- bt_c |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, 7L, 1L),
         tenure = factor(tenure, levels = c("Renter", "Owner")))

town_pts <- bt |>
  filter(geo_type == "place", year == 2024) |>
  flag_reliability() |>
  mutate(
    share = if_else(reliability == "Low", NA_real_, share),
    date  = make_date(year, 7L, 1L),
    town  = geo_label(GEOID),
    tenure = factor(tenure, levels = c("Renter", "Owner")),
    lbl = paste0(town, if_else(reliability == "Medium", "*", ""))
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = trend_c, aes(date, share, color = tenure), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = trend_c, aes(date, share, color = tenure), size = 1.8) +
  geom_point(data = town_pts, aes(date, share, color = tenure),
             shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2.4, stroke = 1) +
  geom_text(data = town_pts, aes(date, share, label = lbl, color = tenure),
            hjust = 0, nudge_x = 60, size = 2.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Renter = coral, Owner = blue), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, NA), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.08))) +
  scale_x_date(breaks = make_date(c(2013, 2017, 2021, 2024), 7L, 1L), date_labels = "%Y",
               expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.18))) +
  labs(
    title = "Cost burden has eased since 2013 but renters remain far more burdened",
    subtitle = "Share of cost-burdened households: <span style='color:#e76f52'>**renters**</span> vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**owners**</span> (open points are 2024 towns)",
    caption = paste0(
      "**Source:** U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, Tables B25070 and B25091, 2013–2024.",
      "<br>**Notes:** Excludes households whose income-to-cost ratio is not computed (about 700 renters).<br>",
      "ACS burden therefore exceeds the CHAS estimate (renters ",
      label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(chas_rent), "). See Data & Methodology. ",
      "\\*Medium reliability (CV 15–30%)."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

Both towns run hotter than the county on renter cost-burden: 55% of Warrenton's renters and almost 59% of Bealeton's renters are cost burdened. These data sit well above the county line (2024).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Town spotlight — Warrenton and Bealeton carry the county's highest renter burden
Both towns run hotter than the county on renter cost burden versus `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(acs_rent_24)` countywide. Warrenton's cell is High reliability, while Bealeton's is Medium (CV 15–30%) and is read as a count-based signal, not a precise rate. As the county's principal rental submarket (@fig-hh-band-tenure), Warrenton concentrates both the renters and the burden — the same submarket where the affordable-rental deficit (@fig-rental-gap) bites hardest.
:::

## The core picture: burden is concentrated at the lowest incomes (CHAS)

Overall, renters are more cost burdened than owners within every income band, and severe burden is especially concentrated among the lowest-income renters: the households with the least disposable income to absorb a rent increase or utility cost change.

Burden collapses onto the bottom of the income ladder. At lower than 30% AMI, the vast majority of both renters and owners are cost-burdened. Most of them are severely cost burdened, meaning these households pay half or more of their income towards housing costs. Conversely, above 80% AMI the cost burden all but disappears for renters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-burden-band
#| fig-cap: "Cost burden is overwhelmingly a low-income problem"
#| fig-alt: "Stacked bar chart of cost burden by AMI income band and tenure for Fauquier County, faceted into renter and owner panels. At 30% AMI and below, the large majority of both renters (about 73%) and owners (about 87%) are cost-burdened, most of them severely. The burdened share falls sharply as income rises, and above 100% AMI fewer than 6% of households in either tenure are burdened. Owners are as burdened as renters or more so in most bands, and renters are more burdened only at 30–50% AMI."

t8_band <- chas$t8 |>
  filter(geo_code == fauquier, cost_burden != "No or negative income") |>
  summarize(estimate = sum(estimate),
            .by = c(household_income, tenure, cost_burden)) |>
  mutate(
    band = factor(household_income, levels = band_lvls),
    tenure = factor(if_else(tenure == "Homeowner", "Owners", "Renters"),
                    levels = c("Renters", "Owners")),
    cost_burden = factor(cost_burden,
                         levels = c("Severely cost-burdened", "Cost-burdened", "Not cost-burdened"))
  ) |>
  mutate(share = estimate / sum(estimate), .by = c(band, tenure))

ggplot(t8_band, aes(band, share, fill = cost_burden)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.74) +
  facet_wrap(~ tenure) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cb_pal) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = band_en) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.03))) +
  labs(
    title = "Cost burden is overwhelmingly a low-income problem",
    subtitle = "Share of households by cost-burden status, income band, and tenure, Fauquier County",
    caption = chas_cap("T8"),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", plot.subtitle = element_markdown(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7, angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Data note: CHAS vs. ACS burden
Measured on the CHAS universe, county burden is `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(chas_rent)` for renters and `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(chas_own)` for owners, lower than the ACS headline (@fig-burden-trend) because CHAS uses a different denominator; the two are reconciled in the Data & Methodology appendix (@sec-data-notes).
:::

## The rental gap: too few homes for the lowest incomes

The deepest shortfall in rentals is among the lowest income bands. The county has about `r format(abs(rg_deficit_30), big.mark = ",")` fewer rentals that are affordable and available to renter households with less than 30% AMI. These are the households with essentially no market alternative.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rental-gap
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("The county is short about ", format(abs(rg_deficit_30), big.mark = ","), " rentals affordable to its lowest-income renters")'
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Diverging horizontal bar chart of the surplus or deficit of affordable and available rental units by AMI band in Fauquier County. Every band shows a deficit. The deepest shortfall relative to renter households is at 30% AMI and below (about ", format(rg_deficit_30, big.mark = ","), " units against ", format(rg$renter_hh[rg$band == "≤30% AMI"], big.mark = ","), " renter households). The largest absolute deficit, about ", format(abs(rg$surplus_deficit[rg$band == ">80% AMI"]), big.mark = ","), " units, is in the combined >80% AMI band.")'

rg_plot <- gaps$rental_gap |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, levels = rev(c("≤30% AMI","30-50% AMI","50-80% AMI",">80% AMI"))))

ggplot(rg_plot, aes(surplus_deficit, band)) +
  geom_col(fill = coral, width = 0.68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_comma()(surplus_deficit),
                hjust = if_else(surplus_deficit < 0, 1.1, -0.1)),
            size = 3.2, color = "grey20") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = band_en) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(),
                     expand = expansion(c(0.16, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("The county is short about ", format(abs(rg_deficit_30), big.mark = ","),
                   " rentals affordable to its lowest-income renters"),
    subtitle = "Affordable and available rentals minus renter households by income band",
    caption = paste0(chas_cap("T14B/T15C"),
                     "<br>**Notes:** Affordable-and-available units are both priced for and occupied at or below the band.<br>",
                     "The >80% AMI band combines the 100% and 120% AMI groups."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE) +
  add_zero_line("x")
```

All income bands run a deficit of rental units for a net shortfall of roughly `r format(abs(rg_deficit_tot), big.mark = ",")` units across the county. As a result, higher-income renters occupy units that would otherwise be affordable to lower-income households, a competition-down-the-ladder dynamic.

The CHAS data behind this gap date to 2018–2022, but more recent lease activity points the same way. Among leases closed through the MLS, the share renting at or below what a 50% AMI household can afford (`r label_dollar()(afford50_rent)`) fell from `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(l50(2022))` in 2022 to `r label_percent(accuracy = 1)(l50(max(lease_50$year)))` in 2026 to date (@sec-market-rental). These broker-placed leases skew toward larger homes, so they overstate typical rents, but the direction of change since the CHAS period is clear.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees described renting in Fauquier as a "gamble": renters need to be quick and involved in the word-of-mouth market to get a decent apartment.
:::

The gap is a supply problem, not a targeting problem: even where units are nominally affordable, they are already occupied with higher income households. This leaves the lowest-income renters with the fewest options. <!-- VERIFY (Amelie comment): "I think we contradict ourselves later" -- re: supply problem vs. targeting problem -->

## The ownership gap: almost nothing for sale below 100% AMI

Below the 100% AMI price ceiling, there is almost nothing for sale: just `r og_below_100` of `r format(og_total_listings, big.mark = ",")` active listings (`r og_asof` snapshot), effectively excluding low to moderate-income buyers. For lower income bands, `r og_lower_txt` active listings are affordable across the 30%, 50%, 80%, and 100% AMI bands.

The overwhelming majority of listings, `r og_top_band` of `r format(og_total_listings, big.mark = ",")`, are priced only within reach of the 120% AMI band or above, mirroring the median-price gap in @tbl-afford-band. Owner-household counts far exceed affordable listings in every income band below the highest wealth households, so first-time and lower-income buyers face a market with essentially no entry point.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ownership-gap
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Only ", og_below_100, " of ", og_total_listings, " active listings are affordable below 100% AMI")'
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Bar chart comparing, for each AMI band, the number of active for-sale listings affordable in that price range against the number of owner households in the band, Fauquier County. Listings affordable below 100% AMI are almost nonexistent (", og_lower_txt, " across the four lower bands), while ", og_top_band, " of the ", og_total_listings, " listings fall only in the 120% AMI price range at the top.")'

og_plot <- gaps$ownership_gap |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, levels = c("ami30","ami50","ami80","ami100","ami120"),
                        labels = c("30% AMI","50% AMI","80% AMI","100% AMI","120% AMI"))) |>
  select(band, `Listings affordable` = listings_affordable, `Owner households` = households) |>
  pivot_longer(-band, names_to = "measure", values_to = "n")

ggplot(og_plot, aes(band, n, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), width = 0.66) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_comma()(n),
                fontface = if_else(measure == "Listings affordable", "bold", "plain")),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.72), vjust = -0.4, size = 2.8, color = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Listings affordable` = coral, `Owner households` = blue)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(c(0, 0.16))) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Only ", og_below_100, " of ", og_total_listings, " active listings are affordable below 100% AMI"),
    subtitle = "<span style='color:#e76f52'>**Active for-sale listings**</span> affordable in each price range vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**owner households**</span> in the band",
    caption = paste0("**Sources:** Bright MLS active for-sale listings, ", mls_through, " snapshot. ",
                     "HUD CHAS, 2018–2022, Table T7.",
                     "<br>**Notes:** Each listing is placed in the AMI price range it falls within. ",
                     "Price ranges follow the assumptions in Table 5.2."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda() +
  add_zero_line("y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.subtitle = element_markdown(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))
```

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Realtors interviewed said they cannot take on clients seeking homes at $250,000 or less, because they know these households will not find success in Fauquier. The buyers who do are dual-income, high-earning households.
:::

## The bottom line: wages don't reach the cost of housing

The all-jobs average wage (`r label_dollar()(wage_all)` annually) narrowly covers the county's median rent (`r label_dollar()(inc_rent)` needed), a margin of about `r label_dollar()(wage_all - inc_rent)`, or roughly 5%. That headline flips, though, once you look sector by sector: Health Care (`r label_dollar()(wage_health)`), Local Government (`r label_dollar()(wage_gov)`), and especially Retail Trade (`r label_dollar()(wage_retail)` yearly) all pay below the `r label_dollar()(inc_rent)` needed. This could lead to greater cost burden for households working in Retail Trade or even the Local Government, or contribute to in and out migration and daily commuting patterns for local workers.

The data bear out that workers cannot afford to both work and live here, most clearly for buying and for the lower-wage sectors: even a two-earner household of two average local jobs (`r label_dollar()(wage_all*2)`) falls well short of the `r label_dollar()(inc_buy)` needed to buy the median priced home. Ownership, not rental, is where the wage-to-cost gap is structural and unavoidable.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wages-costs
#| fig-cap: "The average wage covers rent but no wage path reaches homeownership"
#| fig-alt: !expr 'paste0("Lollipop chart of average annual wages for major Fauquier employment sectors, shown for a single earner and a two-earner household, against two reference lines: the income needed to afford the median rent (about ", label_dollar()(inc_rent), ") and the income needed to buy the median home (about ", label_dollar()(inc_buy), "). The all-jobs average wage of ", label_dollar()(wage_all), " narrowly clears the rent line, but Health Care (", label_dollar()(wage_health), "), Local Government (", label_dollar()(wage_gov), "), and especially Retail Trade (", label_dollar()(wage_retail), ") all fall short of it. No single-earner wage reaches the purchase line; even a two-earner all-jobs household (", label_dollar()(wage_all * 2), ") falls well short of the income needed to buy.")'

wc_plot <- gaps$wages_costs |>
  filter(category != "2-worker household") |>
  select(category, one_earner, two_earner) |>
  pivot_longer(-category, names_to = "earners", values_to = "wage") |>
  mutate(
    earners = if_else(earners == "one_earner", "One earner", "Two earners"),
    category = fct_reorder(category, wage, .fun = max)
  )

ggplot(wc_plot, aes(wage, category)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = inc_rent, color = green, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "22") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = inc_buy,  color = yellow, linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(aes(group = category), color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = earners), size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = inc_rent, y = 4.9, label = "Income needed\nto rent",
           color = green, size = 2.7, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = inc_buy, y = 4.9, label = "Income needed\nto buy",
           color = yellow, fontface = "bold", size = 2.7, hjust = 1.08, vjust = 1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`One earner` = coral, `Two earners` = blue)) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = str_to_sentence, expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1.2))) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"),
                     expand = expansion(c(0.02, 0.08)),
                     limits = c(0, NA)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title = "The average wage covers rent but no wage path reaches homeownership",
    subtitle = "Average annual wage by sector: <span style='color:#e76f52'>**one earner**</span> vs <span style='color:#445ca9'>**two earners**</span><br>Dashed lines show the income needed to <span style='color:#8baeaa'>**rent**</span> and to <span style='color:#e9ab3f'>**buy**</span>",
    caption = paste0(qcew_cap("2025"),
                     "<br>**Notes:** Income needed follows the assumptions in Table 5.2, with rent anchored to the ACS median gross rent."),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_hda(flip_gridlines = TRUE) +
  add_zero_line("x") +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.subtitle = element_markdown())
```

The message is ultimately structural and systemic: the county's wage base and its housing costs have decoupled. Dual-income working households are priced out of the ownership market, while the lowest-wage sectors are priced out of the market entirely - both rentals and ownership opportunities. The wage to housing cost gap is not just a perception. This gap of wages and housing costs has become a defining structural feature of Fauquier's housing market.

::: {.callout-note title="What we heard"}
Interviewees repeatedly emphasized that "Workers cannot afford to both work and live here." Several interviewees shared that they cannot even afford to live in Fauquier despite working there.
:::
